newsitem.title: UK: McDonald's resumes British beef purchases.
newsitem.headline: McDonald's resumes British beef purchases.

text.p: Hamburger chain McDonald's Corp gave Britain's beleaguered farming industry a much-needed boost on Thursday when it announced it was resuming purchases of British beef for sale in its 764 restaurants in the country.
The move, the most significant victory for the industry since the onset of the "mad cow disease" crisis 15 months ago, was immediately hailed by Agriculture Minister Jack Cunningham.
He said it sent a message to other European Union states who have prohibited exports of British beef since March 1996 that they should review the ban speedily.
"It will strengthen our case as we press for the lifting of the ban," Cunningham told a joint news conference with Andrew Taylor, managing director of British McDonald's restaurants.
"We are delighted by the news, which is an important step in the campaign to get British beef back onto the menus of Europe," said Sir David Naish, president of the National Farmers Union.

The EU ban followed new scientific evidence suggesting it was possible for people eating beef from cows suffering from Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy to contract the human version of the brain-wasting malady, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
McDonald's almost immediately said it would make its hamburgers solely from foreign beef.

Taylor said on Thursday the firm had never believed that British beef was not safe to eat, but had been responding to consumer research conducted in March last year showing 70 percent of its customers were not willing to eat it.
"Recovery in confidence has been slow, but the results of our latest research, conducted this month, show that 74 percent of consumers now do want us to sell British beef."
McDonald's decision, which it will announce with full-page advertisements in British newspapers on Friday, will be worth some 30 million pounds ($49.73 million) a year to British beef farmers.
Over half its beef here will now come from British herds.
The Meat and Livestock Commission (MLC) hailed McDonald's decision as a triumph for British livestock.

"British farmers have been through an extremely hard time following the BSE crisis and this will be a great morale boost for them. It is also good news for British consumers who want to eat British beef," MLC director general Colin Maclean said in a statement.

Agriculture Ministry sources said Cunningham will meet one of McDonald's major rivals, Grand Metropolitan Plc 's Burger King, on Tuesday to discuss whether they are now willing to resume purchases of British-raised cattle.

Britain has already slaughtered tens of thousands of cattle in its efforts to convince its European Union partners that it is acting to eradicate BSE and has moved to improve hygiene in its slaughterhouses.

The moves have helped restore confidence in beef among British consumers, with purchases currently running 19 percent above year-ago levels according to the industry body, the Meat and Livestock Commission.
Cunningham has said he may soon tighten controls on imported beef to ensure it comes up to British standards.
But he has warned the industry that he cannot predict a quick lifting of the ban.
